entries.definition: Unweighted power-mean (p=4) of every scouted 20-80 tool a prospect carries, plus FG physical grades - the high exponent rewards extreme tools, so one elite grade lifts the composite more than balanced mediocrity. Expressed on the 20-80 scouting scale.
entries.methodology: Tool is the equally-weighted power-mean (p=4) of every 20-80 tool grade a hitter carries (hit, pwr, run, field, arm, pitch_sel, bat_ctrl) PLUS the FG -2..+2 physical grades (Frame, Athleticism) mapped to the FV scale (-2→30, -1→40, 0→50, +1→60, +2→70). For pitchers the physicals (Frame, Athleticism, Delivery) join the stuff power-mean (p=3) alongside fb/sl/cb/ch, then overall = 0.65·stuff + 0.35·cmd. The p=4 exponent (steeper than the p=3 used by O-Tool and pStuff+) rewards extreme tools more aggressively: a 70 PWR + 45 HIT prospect (arith mean 57.5) posts ~58 here vs ~57.6 under p=3. The output is the raw power-mean on the 20-80 scouting scale - 50 = average, 60 = Plus, 70 = elite (no z-scoring step).
entries.formula:
Tool = (Σ tool_grade^4 / n)^(1/4)
hitter inputs: hit, pwr, run, field, arm, pitch_sel, bat_ctrl, frame_fv, athl_fv
pitcher: Tool = 0.65 · power-mean(fb, sl, cb, ch, frame_fv, athl_fv, delivery_fv; p=3) + 0.35 · cmd
entries.example: A 70 PWR / 45 HIT prospect with otherwise-50 tools posts a Tool around 58 - the p=4 power-mean lifts the composite above the 57.5 arithmetic mean because PWR skews the result.

entries.definition: Weighted offensive composite on the 20-80 scale: HIT 40 / PWR 40 / BCTRL 10 / PSEL 6 / RUN 4.
entries.methodology: O-Tool is the weighted mean of the hitter's offensive 20-80 grades, output directly on the 20-80 scouting scale (50 = avg, 60 = Plus, 70 = elite). Weights reflect the heavy bats-matter-most tilt - HIT and PWR are co-dominant at 40% each; bat-control and pitch-selection round out the offensive profile; speed is a small tiebreaker contributor. Defensive tools (field, arm) live in D-Tool (separate index).
entries.formula:
O-Tool = Σ w_i · grade_i / Σ w_i
weights: HIT 0.40, PWR 0.40, BCTRL 0.10, PSEL 0.06, RUN 0.04
entries.example: A 60 HIT / 60 PWR / 50-elsewhere hitter posts an O-Tool of 58 - both top weights at Plus pull the composite well above average.

entries.definition: Weighted defensive composite (p=3 power-mean) on the 20-80 scale: DEF 60 / ARM 30 / RUN 10 - catchers DEF 70 / ARM 30.
entries.methodology: D-Tool is the weighted power-mean (Lₚ with p=3) of the position player's defensive 20-80 grades, output directly on the 20-80 scouting scale (50 = avg, 60 = Plus, 70 = elite). Defense overwhelmingly drives the composite at 60%; arm strength matters but second-order at 30%; baserunning speed contributes a small 10% (it folds into range/jumps via the field grade already, this is a tiebreaker contributor). Catchers drop speed (irrelevant) and bump field to 70%, since the field grade for catchers absorbs framing/blocking/receiving. The p=3 power-mean rewards elite-glove standouts more sharply than a simple weighted mean.
entries.formula:
D-Tool = (Σ w_i · grade_i^3 / Σ w_i)^(1/3)
non-catcher weights: DEF 0.60, ARM 0.30, RUN 0.10
catcher weights:    DEF 0.70, ARM 0.30 (RUN dropped)
entries.example: A 70 DEF / 50 ARM / 50 RUN center fielder posts a D-Tool near 62; a 50/50/50 baseline lands at 50.

entries.definition: Rare active-prospect flag: tool/FV velocity AND a strong performance gate, with an age cap. Surfaces roughly 10-40 prospects league-wide.
entries.methodology: An active prospect flags as Breakout when ALL of the following hold over the window max(last 6 months, last 4 source updates): (a) consensus FV upgraded by ≥ +5 grade points OR mean tool-grade composite improved by ≥ +3; (b) a strong performance gate fires - hitters: RPS+ ≥ 110 or wRC+ ≥ 130; pitchers: Peripheral Stuff+ ≥ 105 or FIP- ≤ 90 (v29 - Statcast+ ≥ 115 also passes as an alternative gate); (c) v15 age cap - position players and SPs through age 24; relievers (RP / MIRP / SIRP / CL) through age 25 (relievers peak earlier in their development arc, so an aging-relief hot stretch shouldn't read as a prospect breakout). Tuned to surface ~10-40 prospects league-wide. The badge gets an aquamarine pulsing ★ mark (bottom-left corner) with a tooltip explaining which signal fired and which gate passed.
entries.formula:
breakout = (fv_upgrade ≥ +5 OR tool_velocity ≥ +3)
         AND perf_gate_pass
         AND (age ≤ 24 starters/hitters, age ≤ 25 relievers)
entries.visual: 50★→ aquamarine ★ + pulsing bottom edge
entries.example: A 20-year-old A+ hitter whose consensus jumped +5 FV in four months while running RPS+ 118 flags Breakout ★; a 24-year-old AAA arm with the same grade jump does not (age cap), and neither does a riser whose performance gate reads RPS+ 96 (velocity without production is a re-rank, not a breakout).

entries.definition: Soft-pink ^ mark in the top-right corner of an FV badge - at least one source published a '+' upside marker on the latest snapshot.
entries.methodology: Source-side upside note: when an outlet publishes a grade like 45+ / 40+ / 35+, the player carries an Upside indicator. Capped at FV ≤ 50 because 50+ / 55+ / 60+ tiers have already realized their upside (the mark is meant to flag sub-50 prospects with publishable room to climb). The badge gets a soft-pink ^ glyph (top-right corner) plus a pink top-edge accent; tooltip lists which sources added the '+' grade. Surfaces as a 'pink pill' driver chip on the Spotlights page when a source added a '+' in the trailing 6 months. Glyph is ^ (circumflex) so it doesn't visually collide with the health '+' row pill.
entries.visual: 45^→ soft-pink ^ + pink top edge
entries.example: A source publishing 45+ on a 19-year-old shortstop puts the soft-pink ^ on his FV badge: the outlet sees a grade above the number. A 55+ from the same outlet shows no marker because 55 already prices the upside (the cap keeps the mark meaningful below FV 50).

entries.definition: CollegeSavant's tracked-skill index. 100 = the season's college pool average, +10 = one standard deviation better. A college-relative read on tracked skill, not a Single-A projection.
entries.methodology:
A pool-anchored z-average of the TrackMan tracked skills, on the same 100 + 10 x z convention as SC+, computed against the same per-year college cohort the percentile sliders use.

Hitters: two equally-weighted families, contact quality (90th-percentile exit velocity / barrel% / hard-hit%) and plate discipline (zone-contact% / -whiff% / -chase%). Pitchers: stuff and whiffs (Stuff+ / swinging-strike% / induced chase%) and contact suppression (-barrel% / -hard-hit% / -xwOBA against). Components a player or year does not carry simply drop out.

Each component is z-scored against its per-year cohort, sign-adjusted so higher is better, averaged within each family, then the two families are averaged so neither outvotes the other. Rescaled 100 + 10 x z and clamped to 40-160.

It is observation-only (no scouting prior) and college-relative: it says a player is better than the college pool on tracked skill, not that he will produce at Single-A. CollegeSavant's Stuff+ in particular does not predict pro outcomes in the matched data.
entries.formula: CS+ = 100 + 10 × avg(family means of z-scored tracked components vs the per-year college cohort)
entries.example: A hitter at 90th-percentile EV +1.2σ, barrel% +1σ, hard-hit% +0.8σ with average discipline lands near CS+ 115, well above the college pool on tracked skill.

entries.definition: What a college line projects to against Single-A pitching, shown as an expected value plus a P10-P90 uncertainty band. A matched-pair projection, not a precise forecast.
entries.methodology: Built from our own data: each CollegeSavant player is joined by name to draft_players and their later Single-A (A / A+) statline in prospects.db. Per stat, a regression-to-the-mean is fit over the matched pairs (predicted = the Single-A mean + a shrunk slope x (college value - the college mean)), so a weak relationship pulls hard toward the level mean. Only K% and BB% live on BOTH the college tracked side and the Single-A side, so those are the matched-pair translation; hitter OPS (from college xwOBA) is shipped EXPERIMENTAL because college tracked data barely forecasts Single-A production in the sample. The band is the P10-P90 residual range and widens with thinner support; leave-one-out coverage runs near the 80% target. NOT adjusted for strength of schedule or park (no conference / park table is held). K% is the most reliable output; BB% and OPS carry little signal and are flagged. Stuff+ does not predict Single-A outcomes in the matched data, so the pitcher translation is K% / BB% only and the tracked skills stay the descriptive CS+ index.
entries.formula: proj_single_a = single_a_mean + shrunk_slope x (college_value - college_mean); band = P10-P90 of the fit residuals
entries.example: A college hitter with a 12% strikeout rate projects to about a 19% Single-A rate with an 80% band near 11-27%: contact tends to erode against pro pitching, and the band reflects how much the jump varies player to player.

entries.definition: Pool-anchored composite of tracked Statcast / zone signals. 100 = pool mean; ≥105 reads as above-pool, ≤95 below-pool, ≥120 elite.
entries.methodology:
Side-aware blend of the per-prospect tracked-data signal. Hitters: contact quality (avg exit velocity / hard-hit% / barrel%) + zone discipline (z-contact% / -whiff% / -chase%). Pitchers: top-pitch avg velocity + induced whiffs + induced chase + (inverted) hard-hit allowed + barrel allowed.

Each component is z-scored against the side-matched active pool, averaged, then rescaled so 100 = pool mean and one population stddev moves the index 15 points (wRC+/OPS+ family). Powers: (a) the SC+ filter chip on the Active list, (b) a colored 'SC+' driver chip on the Spotlights page (green ≥105 / red ≤95 / yellow neutral), (c) a tiebreak inside fvCmpDesc when two prospects share an FV + upside flag, (d) faller + rebounder confirmation/contradiction in the Spotlights bucket scoring, (e) a per-side hitter/pitcher SC+ aggregate on each farm-system page.

None when the player has no tracked Statcast / zone data on any component.
entries.formula: SC+ = 100 + 15 × avg(z-scored components vs side-matched pool)
entries.example: A hitter with EV 92 (+1σ), HH% 45 (+1σ), Z-Con% 88 (+0.5σ) lands around SC+ 113 - solidly above-pool, reads green in driver chips.
entries.visual: SC+ 122SC+ 101SC+ 84

entries.definition: 0–100 composite that separates two prospects carrying the IDENTICAL FV grade by projected MLB success. Cohort-aware (MiLB / Draft / Overseas) and injury-aware.
entries.methodology:
When two prospects share the same Future Value, raw FV can't separate them - TBS does. It blends scouting grades, cohort-normalized performance, and developmental/risk modifiers into one 0–100 number, tuned per cohort for 'how likely is this player to become a useful MLB regular?' rather than current-season output.

MiLB (active): Tool composite 26% · RPS+ 16% · SC+ 16% · per-tool max 10% · Stuff+ 8% (pitchers) · age-vs-level 8% · health/injuries 10% · stock movement 6%. MLB Draft: Draft Stock+ 27% · Tool+ 18% · college RPS+ 17% · Tool composite 10% · per-tool max 10% · age 8% · health 6% · movement 4%.

Overseas: Tool+ 22% · cohort RPS+ 18% · translation-adjusted wRC+ or FIP 18% · Tool composite 8% · per-tool max 8% · age 4% · health 4% · movement 4%. Each signal is independently normalized to 0–1 and clipped; any missing signal drops out and the remaining weights renormalize, so a partial-data player still scores on a comparable scale.

The HEALTH term works the same way everywhere: a prospect currently on the IL zeros it (sinking below a healthy same-FV peer); recent IL history (≥1 stint or ≥30 days in the trailing year) or a post-Tommy-John recovery window partially discounts it; a clean profile is neutral-max. TBS drives same-FV ordering on the Draft + Overseas lists, the surplus-value nudge in trade evaluations, and the 'TBS NN' line in Trade Audit cards.

The Active list's headline #overall-rank is computed server-side with a matching FV → Tools → currently-on-IL tiebreak, so an injured prospect also ranks just behind a healthy same-FV, same-tools peer there.
entries.formula: TBS = round( 100 × Σ(signalᵢ × weightᵢ) ÷ Σ(weightᵢ for present signals) ) - per-cohort weights as listed above
entries.example: Two 50-FV shortstops with similar tools: one healthy (RPS+ 118), one on the 60-day IL. The healthy bat scores ~8–10 TBS points higher and ranks ahead in any same-FV tiebreak.

entries.definition: Level-relative rate index (100 = level average). For active prospects this surfaces the level-anchored OPS+; draft/overseas cohorts compute a cohort-relative z-score.
entries.methodology:
RPS+ is a level-relative rate index. v-arkmetric-audit (implementation status, disclosed): the standalone per-prospect rps_plus field is currently populated only for the DRAFT cohort (100 + 15·z of college-performance) and the OVERSEAS cohort (z vs the international cohort). For ACTIVE MiLB prospects the rps_plus field is not yet computed, so the board falls back to the level-relative OPS+ index (ops_plus_level), the level anchor at the core of RPS+ and the populated relative-performance signal for the active pool.

The fuller design (age × position-group cohort normalization + position multipliers described below) is wired for the cohort exports but not yet for actives; until it is, treat active RPS+ as level-relative OPS+. Intended design: cohort = (age × position group); a small position multiplier (C ×1.08, MI ×1.05, CF ×1.04, 1B ×0.95, DH ×0.92) applied after cohort normalization; MLB-level prospects substitute wRC+ / FIP-.

Note: draft RPS+ is a z-score (×15) while the active OPS+ fallback is a ratio - scale convention differs across the cohort sources.
entries.formula: RPS+ = 100 × (player_score + 100) / (cohort_mean + 100) × position_multiplier · clamped [0, 250]
entries.example: A 21yo catcher and a 21yo 1B with identical OPS+ vs level read at different RPS+ - catcher gets ×1.08, first-baseman ×0.95.

entries.definition: Farm-system development index; 100 = league-mean FV growth. Drives the Development component of the farm report card.
entries.methodology: wRC+-style index for organizational development. Measures each farm's cumulative FV growth over a window (1y / 3y / 6y) and scores it against the league-mean farm. Acquisitions are nullified (a trade-in adds zero to the source farm) and graduations don't subtract; pure development of prospects already in the system. 100 = league mean, 10 pts = 1 stdev across the 30 orgs. The blended trajectory_score that drives the farm letter grade weights the 6y window 60%, 3y 30%, and 1y 10% - 6y is the principal multi-cycle signal; shorter windows still react to the current cycle so a hot current year isn't fully ignored.
entries.formula:
DvM+ = 100 + 10 · (org_growth − league_mean_growth) / league_stdev
blended trajectory_score = 0.60·6y + 0.30·3y + 0.10·1y
entries.example: An org with a 6yDvM+ of 130 has grown its prospects' aggregate FV 3 stdev faster than the average farm system over the last 6 years, after stripping out acquisitions.

entries.definition: Lifetime change in a prospect's consensus tool grade - first observation to latest.
entries.methodology: Per-tool lifetime delta computed across a prospect's full consensus history. For each tool with ≥2 published consensus snapshots, we record first_grade, last_grade, and delta = (last − first). Powers the +N / -N chip beside each tool grade in the prospect-detail Tools section, the Tool development table on the same page, and the org-level rollups (HitDvM+, PowerDvM+, …, ToolDvM+) on the farm-detail page. Tools observed only once produce no delta - that's a 'not enough signal' state, not a 'no change' state.
entries.formula: tool_delta(tool) = consensus_grade_latest(tool) − consensus_grade_first(tool)
entries.example: Jesús Made's game-power tool was 30 in the FG 2024 pre-season and 60 by the 2026 pre-season report - a +30 lifetime delta over 12 observations.

entries.definition: Org-level tool development composite, weighted by what matters per position. 100 = league-mean dev pace; +10 = 1σ above.
entries.methodology:
Position-weighted blend of every per-tool DvM+ an org has populated (HitDvM+, PowerDvM+, SpeedDvM+, FieldDvM+, ArmDvM+, PitchSelDvM+, BatCtrlDvM+ for hitters; FBDvM+, SLDvM+, CBDvM+, CHDvM+, CmdDvM+, CtDvM+ for pitchers). Each per-tool DvM+ is the league-anchored (100 + 10·z) score of an org's mean lifetime tool delta across its multi-cycle actives. v35 - rather than a flat average across tools, ToolDvM+ now weights each tool by its IMPORTANCE for the position bucket the prospect plays: a catcher's Field/Arm count most, an outfielder's Speed, a starter's Fastball/Command.

The composite is computed per bucket (C / INF / OF / SP / RP) using the bucket's own per-tool DvM+ (falling back to the org-wide value when a bucket cell is sparse), then blended across buckets by how many prospects the org actually develops in each. This rewards orgs that grow the tools that MATTER for a position over ones that pad the average with off-position gains.

FG physical grades (Frame, Athleticism, Delivery) are excluded - static published values without the multi-snapshot history DvM+ velocity requires. Attribution: current org - trade-acquired prospects bring their full lifetime delta with them.

Standalone display metric for now; not yet folded into farm_score.
entries.formula:
ToolDvM+ = Σ_bucket (n_bucket · ToolDvM+_bucket) / Σ_bucket n_bucket
ToolDvM+_bucket = Σ_tool (w_tool · DvM+_tool) / Σ_tool w_tool
where w_tool is the tool's position-importance weight for that bucket
entries.example: An org that develops Field + Arm for its catchers and Fastball + Command for its starters scores higher than an equal-on-average org whose gains came from low-importance tools. NYM ToolDvM+ = 106 (rank 1 of 30) ≈ 0.6σ faster development on position-relevant tools than the league-mean farm.

entries.definition: Per-tool org development index. 100 = league mean; +10 = 1σ. Reveals which tools the org actually develops well.
entries.methodology: Same wRC+ shape as DvM+ and ToolDvM+ but scoped to a single tool. For each tool group (Hit, Power = mean of game_pwr + raw_pwr, Speed, Field, Arm, PitchSel, BatCtrl, FB, SL, CB, CH, Cmd, Ct), we compute every org's mean lifetime delta across its actives that have ≥2 consensus observations of that tool, then anchor the league at 100 + 10·z. Cell renders ' - ' for orgs with fewer than 3 prospects contributing - not enough signal to compare. Read these to find a farm's development specialties: HitDvM+ 115 means this org grows the hit tool 1.5σ better than the typical farm.
entries.formula: ToolDvM+ = 100 + 10 · (org_mean_lifetime_delta − league_mean) / league_stdev
entries.example: MIL HitDvM+ 119 + PowerDvM+ 124 = a power-bat development specialist; their hitters add ~2σ more game power across their org tenure than the league mean.

entries.definition: Hit-tool index - weighted blend of performance (AVG + contact), Statcast (zone-contact + whiff), and the Hit/Bat-Control grade. 100 = average.
entries.methodology: Isolates the hit-tool dimension (distinct from POW+ power and OPS+ overall) as a reliability-weighted blend, base 45% PERFORMANCE / 25% STATCAST / 30% Hit-tool. The performance (0.6 · batting-average-vs-level + 0.4 · K%-avoidance-vs-level) and Statcast (zone-contact, whiff) components are down-weighted by sample reliability - batting average is slow to stabilize, so performance is anchored at 170 PA; zone signals stabilize over roughly 200 tracked pitches - so a thin-sample prospect leans on the scouting prior. Batting average and K%-avoidance are distinct contact constructs (not as collinear as ISO+/HR-rate+ in POW+), so the performance core keeps both. Hit grade = mean of Hit and Bat Control on the 20-80 scale (50 → 100, ±10 ≈ ±20). Statcast pool anchors (z-contact ≈ 80%, whiff ≈ 26%) are placeholders pending per-level MiLB calibration.
entries.formula:
HIT+ = Σ wᵢ·xᵢ / Σ wᵢ
perf:     x = 100·(0.6·AVG_ratio + 0.4·contact_ratio),  w = 0.45 · AB/(AB+170)
statcast: x = 0.5·Zcon/80 + 0.5·26/Whiff (×100),  w = 0.25 · pitches/(pitches+200)
tool:     x = 100 + (mean(Hit,BatCtrl) − 50)·2,  w = 0.30  (prior)
entries.example: A AA hitter batting .300 (level .246), 16% K% (level 22.5%), 82% zone-contact, paired with 55 Hit / 60 Bat Control - perf ~133, statcast ~103, tool+ 115 → HIT+ ~122.

entries.definition: Isolated power indexed to the level-average ISO. 100 = league-average; +1 pt = 1% better (wRC+/ERA+ paradigm).
entries.methodology: ISO (SLG − AVG) rescaled against the current level's average ISO so power reads on one cross-level axis: 100 is exactly league-average, 120 is 20% above, 80 is 20% below. The baseline is the same DATA.level_norms cohort every other '+' metric uses (same season/level source). Pure performance rescaling, EMPIRICAL-BAYES shrunk toward the level average by AB (ISO stabilizes ~150 PA), so a 40-AB hot streak no longer posts an extreme ISO+. No scouting-tool blend - that distinguishes it from POW+, which reliability-weights ISO+ with the Power grade and Statcast. Hitters only, 40-game minimum.
entries.formula: ISO+ = 100 + (100·ISO/level_avg_ISO − 100) · AB/(AB+150)   (empirical-Bayes shrunk toward the level average by AB)
entries.example: A High-A hitter with a .180 ISO at a level averaging .130 posts an ISO+ of ~138 (38% above league-average power).

entries.definition: Hitter power index - RELIABILITY-WEIGHTED blend of ISO+ (performance), Statcast (hard-hit + barrel), and the Power grade. The scouting grade anchors thin samples; observed stats take over as PA accrue. 100 = average.
entries.methodology:
Reliability-weighted blend, base importances 45% PERFORMANCE / 25% STATCAST / 30% Power grade. The performance and Statcast components are down-weighted by their own sample reliability - ISO stabilizes around 150 PA, batted-ball quality in tens of batted balls - so a thin-sample prospect leans on the scouting prior and a full-season one leans on observed power.

The performance signal is ISO+ ALONE: the prior version also summed an HR-rate+ term, but ISO+ and HR-rate+ correlate 0.91 across active hitters, so adding them double-counted one power trait and inflated the reading. Validated against graduate outcomes - the reliability-weighted POW+ predicts MLB ISO at 0.50, up from 0.35.

Power grade on the 20-80 scale (50 → 100, ±10 ≈ ±20). Statcast pool anchors (hard-hit ≈ 33%, barrel ≈ 6%) remain placeholders pending per-level MiLB calibration.
entries.formula:
POW+ = Σ wᵢ·xᵢ / Σ wᵢ
perf:     x = ISO+,  w = 0.45 · AB/(AB+150)
statcast: x = 0.55·HH%/33 + 0.45·Brl%/6 (×100),  w = 0.25 · BBE/(BBE+40)
tool:     x = 100 + (Power_grade − 50)·2,  w = 0.30  (prior, full weight)
entries.example: A AA hitter with ISO+ 145, hard-hit 40% / barrel 9% (statcast ~134), and a 60 Power grade (tool+ 120) → POW+ ~135.

entries.definition: Plate-discipline index; BB% minus K% differential vs level-mean blended 70/30 with the Pitch-Selection (PSel) tool. 100 = average.
entries.methodology: The raw component is an additive shift on the BB% minus K% differential vs the player's level mean: 100 + (player_diff − level_diff). A hitter walking 10% and striking out 20% (−10 diff) at a level where the mean is +5% BB minus 22% K (−17 diff) posts a raw 107. That raw index is then blended 70% / 30% with the player's Pitch-Selection (PSel) scouting grade - FanGraphs' plate-discipline tool - on the 20-80 scale (50 → 100, ±10 grade ≈ ±20 points). Hitters only, 40-game minimum. Below the sample gate a graded prospect gets the tool alone; with no PSel grade the raw stats stand alone. (Renamed from Disci+.)
entries.formula:
PD+ = 0.7 · raw + 0.3 · tool+
raw = 100 + (BB%player − K%player) − (BB%level − K%level)
tool+ = 100 + (PSel_grade − 50) · 2
entries.example: Juan Soto's career-prospect raw PD+ would have been ~125-130 (BB%−K% ~25 points above the typical bat); paired with a plus PSel grade the blended PD+ holds in that same elite band.

entries.definition: Peripheral pitcher index; K%, BB%, HR/9 vs level mean. 100 = league-average peripherals.
entries.methodology: Z-score composite of three workload-stable peripheral rates: strikeout rate (positive), walk rate (negative), and HR/9 (negative), each normalized to the pitcher's current level mean with an approximate σ = 15% of mean. K% and BB% are per-batter rates so a reliever's stuff reads the same way relative to a starter's, unlike K/9 which over-rewards short-outing relievers. 10 points ≈ 1 stdev. Pitchers only, 20-IP or 30-BF sample gate. (Renamed from STF+ - the 'p' prefix marks it as the peripheral version, contrasting with FVStuff+ which scores scouting-grade stuff.)
entries.example: A AA pitcher running a 30% K%, 7% BB%, 0.8 HR/9 at a level where the means are 22% / 9% / 1.0 posts a pStuff+ around 125, well-above-average peripherals for the level.

entries.definition: In-house pitch-quality model for AAA pitchers; scores per-pitch kinematics against run value. 100 = qualified-AAA pool mean, 10 pts = 1 stdev, higher = better stuff.
entries.methodology:
The platform's first in-house pitch-quality model, built to score stuff for pitchers who have not debuted (external Stuff+ models only cover MLB tracking). A LightGBM regressor is trained on Savant minors per-pitch detail (AAA, 2023 onward) to predict each pitch's run value from physics alone: velocity, spin, extension, arm-side-signed horizontal and vertical movement, release point, arm angle, and the velocity gap off the pitcher's primary fastball. No pitch-type labels and no results enter the features, so the score reads raw stuff, not usage or sequencing.

A pitcher's score is his season mean predicted run value, shrunk toward the pool mean below 300 pitches, then scaled so 100 is the qualified-AAA pool mean and 10 points is one standard deviation. The model is validated season-out (train 2023-24, score 2025 out-of-sample) and gated forward against graduates' first-MLB outcomes; the eval ships in data/stuff_plus_aaa_eval.json whatever it says.

Differs from pStuff+ (peripheral results: K%, BB%, HR/9 vs level mean) and FVStuff+ (scouting-grade composite): aStuff+ measures the pitches themselves from tracking data.
entries.formula:
aStuff+ = 100 + 10 · (μ_pool − RV̂_shrunk) / σ_pool
where RV̂_shrunk = (n · RV̂ + 300 · μ_pool) / (n + 300)
entries.example: A AAA starter whose pitches grade 1 stdev better than the qualified pool over 1,500 tracked pitches posts an aStuff+ around 110; the same stuff over 150 pitches reads closer to 103 until the sample grows.

entries.definition: Scouting-grade pitch composite; power-mean of fastball + secondaries grades, z-scored across the prospect cohort.
entries.methodology: Outlier-biased composite (Lₚ with p=3) of the pitcher's 20-80 grades on Fastball + Slider + Curveball + Changeup, then z-scored across the active-prospect cohort. 100 = cohort mean, 10 pts = 1 stdev. Different from pStuff+, which measures results (K%, BB%, HR/9) against level peers; FVStuff+ measures projected stuff from scouting reports. The two can diverge when results outrun (or lag) the underlying scouting view. (Renamed from 'Stuff grade+' - the 'FV' prefix signals it's anchored to the FV-grade scale, contrasting with pStuff+'s peripheral-stats anchoring.)
entries.formula:
FVStuff+ = 100 + 10 · (composite_stuff − μ) / σ
where composite_stuff = (Σ pitch_grade^3 / n)^(1/3)
entries.example: A pitcher with 70 fastball / 60 slider / 55 curve / 50 change posts a composite around 62; if the prospect-cohort mean is 55 and σ is 6, FVStuff+ ≈ 112.

entries.definition: Per-prospect expected MLB surplus value ($M) re-derived from FV→WAR + non-linear $/WAR. Granular to fractional FV (e.g. FV 47.3).
entries.methodology:
v32.1 - Re-anchored to the 2026 FanGraphs scouting primer (FV→peak-WAR ranges, hitter/pitcher split) and the 2026 'What Are Teams Paying for a Win in Free Agency' article (non-linear 3-tier $/WAR, rolling 3yr avg). Formula is now fully decomposed and FV-granular: every input - WAR_peak, success_prob, ramp factor, position multiplier - interpolates between the framework's 5-pt anchors, AND the $/WAR tier dispatches off the interpolated WAR (so the tier transition between FV 45 and FV 50 lands at the right place instead of being smoothed away).

A 47-FV prospect now reads as ~$8M, not ~$13M (which is what naive interp between FV 45's $4M and FV 50's $26M would produce). Hitters carry more than pitchers at equal FV (injury + role-conversion attrition); position scarcity multipliers layered on top.

APPLIES TO PROSPECTS ONLY - debutants/MLB players use realized career_war × $/WAR_overall instead (see surplus_value). NOTE: distinct from OrgSur+, the farm-level capital-efficiency index.
entries.formula:
Sur+ = (WAR_peak(fv) × 6 × ramp × p_success(fv) × $/WAR_tier(WAR_peak) − cost_basis) × position_mult
Anchor points (hitter, pre-position): FV 80→$326M, 70→$212M, 60→$112M, 55→$56M, 50→$26M, 47→$8M, 45→$4M
entries.example: An FV 55 SS: WAR_peak 2.9 × 6 × 0.78 × 0.45 × $13.63M − cost ≈ $56M gross × 1.18 SS mult ≈ $66M Sur+. An FV 47 hitter: WAR_peak 1.49 (interpolated) × ramp × prob × $8.76M (1-2 tier, NOT $13.63M) ≈ $8M Sur+ - properly distinct from FV 45's $4M, not bucketed.

entries.definition: Graduate metric: career WAR per MLB season minus the FV-grade-implied WAR/season baseline.
entries.methodology:
v16 - WAG is matched to the number of MLB SEASONS a graduate has accrued, not plate appearances / rate of production: career WAR ÷ MLB seasons, minus the FV-implied per-season WAR baseline. An injury-shortened season still counts as a season, so WAG reflects accumulation over time rather than a small-sample rate projected up to a full season (which over-credited injury-limited grads like Evan Carter - 5.6 WAR over 4 partial seasons reads on-grade for a 60 FV, not as a 99th-percentile boom).

An elite single season (e.g. Junior Caminero) still posts a high per-season WAG; the BOOM/BUST pill's own sample floor (≥2 MLB seasons OR ≥800 career PA OR ≥200 career IP) holds partial-season grads at 'unsettled'.

WAG sample floor: hitters need ≥150 career PA, pitchers ≥50 career IP - below that, WAG returns None.
entries.formula:
WAG = (career_war / mlb_seasons) − expected_war_per_season(FV)
BOOM ≥ +2.5 · BUST ≤ −1.5 · floor: ≥2 seasons OR ≥800 PA OR ≥200 IP
entries.example: Evan Carter: 5.6 WAR over 4 MLB seasons = 1.4 WAR/season. FV 60 expects ~1.57/season. WAG ≈ −0.2 → SETTLED (on grade).

entries.definition: Graduate metric: WAR/year + WAG/year - combines raw production with grade-beating.
entries.methodology: WARWAG sums a debuted player's playing-time-weighted WAR/year and their WAG/year (WAR Above Grade). Because WAG = WAR/yr − FV-implied WAR/yr, WARWAG works out to (2 × WAR/yr − FV-implied WAR/yr): it rewards graduates who are BOTH genuinely productive (high WAR/yr) AND outperforming the bet implied by their prospect grade (high WAG). A productive player who merely met an elite grade scores lower than an equally-productive player who beat a modest grade. Shares WAG's sample gate - requires ≥1 full-season equivalent of MLB playing time (PA for hitters, IP for pitchers) and an FV on file, else it returns None and the row sinks in the WARWAG sort. Surfaced as a sort (high/low) on the Debuted (Graduates) list; the value shows on each row when that sort is active.
entries.formula: WARWAG = WAR/yr + WAG/yr = 2 · WAR/yr − expected_war(FV)
entries.example: Bobby Witt Jr.: ~6.5 WAR/yr, FV-55 expects ~2.5 → WAG ≈ +4.0, WARWAG ≈ 6.5 + 4.0 = 10.5 (elite on both axes). A 2.5 WAR/yr player who exactly met an FV-55 grade has WAG ≈ 0 → WARWAG ≈ 2.5.

entries.definition: Single source of truth for FV↔WAR↔$ conversions. Prospects flow FV→proj-WAR→proj-$; debutants/MLB use realized WAR→$ (these are kept distinct, never mixed in a single ratio).
entries.methodology:
v32.1 - Consolidated all FV↔WAR↔$ math into one module (value_framework.py) anchored to two Fangraphs sources: the 2026 scouting primer (FV→peak-WAR ranges, hitter/pitcher split) and the 2026 'What Are Teams Paying for a Win in Free Agency' article (non-linear 3-tier $/WAR). Replaces the prior flat $8M/WAR + 2019 Craig Edwards surplus table that powered Sur+, OrgSur+, trade audits, draft pool efficiency, etc. The framework is fully decomposed (every input is auditable + configurable) AND fully granular (interpolates at any FV, not just 5-pt anchors - see Sur+ for the FV 47 example). Backend (storage.py, mlb_trade_lookup.py) and frontend (index.html) read from the SAME generated snapshot (data/value_framework.json + .js) so the two surfaces can never drift again.

CORE PRINCIPLE (v32.1): the framework strictly separates the TWO different valuation regimes:
• **Prospects** (pre-debut, FV grade): valued via FV→projected_WAR→projected_$ using the full formula below. Inherently a PROJECTION.
• **Debutants / MLB players** (post-debut, career_war on file): valued via actual_WAR × $/WAR_overall. A REALIZED figure.
These are never mixed in the same per-FV ratio. Trade audits show projected-$ (prospects) and realized-$ (vets) side-by-side, not combined into a single $/FV.
entries.formula:
Prospect: Surplus($M) = (WAR_peak(fv) × 6 × ramp × p_success(fv) × $/WAR_tier(WAR_peak) − pre_arb − arb_cost) × position_mult
Vet: Value($M) = career_war × $/WAR_overall (≈ $11.74M, rolling 3yr 2024-2026)
entries.example: FV 60 SS hitter (prospect): WAR_peak 4.15 × 6 × 0.78 × 0.62 × $13.63M − costs ≈ $112M × 1.18 SS mult ≈ $133M projected Sur+. Bobby Witt Jr (vet): 22.5 career WAR × $11.74M ≈ $264M realized value. Both true; both distinct.

entries.definition: Non-linear 3-tier $M/WAR price the FA market is paying - fringe / mid / star - rolling 3yr avg. Used tier-aware for per-player; overall rate for career aggregates.
entries.methodology:
Per the 2026 'What Are Teams Paying for a Win in Free Agency' article, teams pay non-linearly for projected first-year WAR. The star premium has roughly doubled vs 2020-2023, so a flat $/WAR mis-prices both ends. The framework uses a rolling 3yr (2024-2026) average across the article's three tiers, dispatched off the player's projected per-year WAR. Two consumption patterns:
• **Per-prospect surplus** (Sur+): the tier dispatches off WAR_peak (FV→WAR), so an FV 47 (~1.5 peak WAR) gets the $8.76M 1-2 tier rate, NOT a linear interp between FV 45 and FV 50.
• **Career WAR for vets**: uses the OVERALL rate ($11.74M) rather than tiers because career WAR aggregates production across multiple seasons at varying tiers, so the overall mean is the appropriate rate.
Used everywhere a $ value is needed: prospect surplus calcs, trade audit valuations, contract surplus comparisons.

Since the v3 re-anchor the tier rates rescale at load to the FA signings-implied level (trailing 3 winters; shape preserved) - one market, one price of a win, shared by prospect surplus, FA rational value, and MLB Projections.
entries.formula:
$/WAR ≈ $6.97M (0-1 WAR) · $8.76M (1-2) · $13.63M (2+) · $11.74M overall (rolling 2024-2026)
Per-prospect: dispatches off WAR_peak. Per-vet: uses overall.
entries.example: A 4-WAR star earns $13.63M per WAR (tier-aware); a fringe 0.5-WAR vet earns $6.97M (tier-aware). A 30-WAR career: 30 × $11.74M overall = $352M (career-aggregate, not tier-aware). The overall rate avoids over-pricing aging vets whose late-career production lives in lower tiers.

entries.definition: Per-FV expected WAR/year, anchored to the FanGraphs scouting primer. The conversion that turns a scouting grade into projected production.
entries.methodology: Each FV grade maps to an expected annual WAR over the player's first six cost-controlled seasons (the years a prospect is an asset). v38 moved the anchor from a single peak-year projection to a 6-year-average WAR and uses one FV-keyed table - no separate hitter/pitcher split, since the side difference is carried later by the position multiplier rather than the WAR anchor. Half-grades linear-interpolate between the 5-pt anchors. This table drives every downstream conversion: surplus value, Sur+, $/FV-pt, and the projected career WAR behind the trade-regret view.
entries.example: An FV 55 prospect projects ~2.5 WAR/yr across the six controlled years; FV 60 jumps to ~3.0. Multiplying by $/WAR and netting the cost basis yields the surplus dollars shown on the card.

entries.definition: Per-FV probability of a prospect becoming an MLB regular (≥2 career WAR). Pitchers run 5-10pp lower than hitters.
entries.methodology: Industry-standard prospect-success rates anchored to Sickels (2002-2012) + McDaniel/Longenhagen (2014-2020) + recent BA primer commentary. Defines 'MLB regular' as accumulating ≥2 career WAR. Pitchers run ~5-10pp lower at each grade due to TJ + role-conversion attrition. These probabilities feed every prospect's expected-WAR-over-6yr calc, which is what makes Sur+ defensible at the upper tail (a FV 70 hitter's ~80% success rate is what gets you to a 9-figure surplus expectation). Configurable in value_framework.py - when our own grad data accumulates enough sample we can override individual cells.
entries.example: An FV 50 hitter has ~32% chance to clear ≥2 career WAR; an FV 50 pitcher ~25%. The 7pp gap propagates into ~25% lower Sur+ for pitchers at every grade.

entries.definition: Translates a prospect's FV grade to a per-point dollar value - surplus_value / FV. PROSPECT-ONLY (vets don't have a meaningful per-FV rate; their value is realized career WAR × $/WAR_overall).
entries.methodology: v32.1 - The bridge between scouting grades and trade-market dollars FOR PROSPECTS ONLY. Per-prospect: $/FV = Sur+ / FV (after position multiplier, after granular FV interpolation - so a 47.3-FV doesn't bucket to FV 45). For a trade audit side: sum the PROSPECT-only $ and PROSPECT-only FV, then divide. Vet $ (realized career_war × $/WAR_overall ≈ $11.74M) is reported SEPARATELY and does NOT contribute to the $/FV ratio - mixing them would conflate a projection with a realized figure. Useful for: comparing trade sides at a glance (which side paid more per FV-pt of cost-controlled prospects?), benchmarking player valuations across orgs.
entries.formula:
Per-prospect: $/FV-pt = Sur+ / FV
Per trade-side: $/FV-pt = Σ(prospect_$) / Σ(prospect_FV)  (vet $ reported separately)
entries.example: An FV 60 SS Sur+ ~$133M → $2.2M/FV-pt (prospect). A trade where Org A receives 15 FV worth $25M of prospects + 1 vet worth $48M shows: '15 FV @ $1.7M/FV + $48M (1 vet)' - never combined as $73/15 = $4.9M/FV (that would be apples-and-oranges).

entries.definition: Active prospects' current FV per $M of trailing-3yr draft-pool spend. Fast-cycle companion to war_per_m_pool.
entries.methodology: v32.0 - Companion to Draft Pool Efficiency's WAR/$M signal. Where war_per_m_pool sums grad career WAR over (T-5)..(T-2) drafts and lags reality by ~5yr (the WAR maturation window), fv_per_m_pool sums the CURRENT consensus FV of ACTIVE prospects from the same draft years and reads as fast as the next ranking cycle. Both signals share the same denominator (the org's pool $ for the window), so a high fv_per_m / low war_per_m gap is a leading indicator: the scouting + dev are working but the WAR hasn't shown up yet. The reverse (high war / low fv) suggests grad-side success isn't being replenished. Gated only on pool > $0.
entries.formula: fv_per_m_pool = Σ(active_fv | drafted T-5..T-2) / (org_pool_$ T-5..T-2 / 1M)
entries.example: Org X spent $35M of draft pool over T-5..T-2 and has 280 FV-pts in active prospects from those drafts → 8.0 FV/$M. Concurrent war_per_m might still be 0 (grads haven't matured), but the scouting/dev signal already reads high.

entries.definition: Org-level $ surplus per FV-point of active prospect capital. Captures the quality-of-FV-mix dimension.
entries.methodology: v32.0 - Sub-metric inside the fin_active_surplus leaf. Divides the org's total active-prospect Sur+ ($M) by the org's total active-prospect FV-pts. High = the FV is concentrated in high-leverage positions (SS, CF, premium SP) and/or high-FV grades where the surplus curve is steep. Low = depth-heavy but flat (lots of FV 45-50 corner / bench profiles). Lets two orgs with the same raw FV-pts be differentiated by whether their portfolio is star+premium-position or generic depth. Gated at ≥5 contributing actives.
entries.formula: surplus_per_fv_pt_mm = Σ(Sur+ across actives) / Σ(FV across same actives)
entries.example: Org A (LAD-style top-loaded) has 250 active FV-pts and $400M surplus → $1.6M/FV-pt. Org B (depth-style) has 400 active FV-pts but $300M surplus → $0.75M/FV-pt. Same raw quality dial reads differently in $/FV space.

entries.definition: Starting pitcher - projects to start games (typically 5+ innings per outing).
entries.methodology: Starting Pitcher. Carries the bulk of the workload - 5+ innings per outing in a 5-man rotation. Projection requires 3+ quality offerings (arsenal depth) AND command good enough to face a lineup multiple times. SP-projected prospects typically receive higher FV grades than relief-projected arms of similar raw stuff because innings count more than leverage on the WAR ledger. Filter chip `SP` matches only SP-tagged prospects (excludes SIRP / MIRP / bare RP).

entries.definition: Relief pitcher - generic relief role. Rolls up SIRP + MIRP + bare RP for filtering.
entries.methodology: Relief Pitcher. The 'RP' filter chip is a rollup: it matches single-inning relievers (SIRP - closer / setup), multi-inning relievers (MIRP - bulk / long-relief), and bare-RP prospects whose role isn't yet specified. Useful when you want every relief-role pitcher in the same view without caring about leverage tier. Use the SIRP / MIRP chips directly when the high-leverage vs bulk distinction matters.

entries.definition: Single-Inning Relief Pitcher - closer or high-leverage setup role (~1 inning per outing).
entries.methodology: Single-Inning Relief Pitcher. FanGraphs designates a pitcher SIRP when their projected role is one-inning, high-leverage relief - closer, setup, fireman. Typically prospects with above-average fastball velocity + at least one plus secondary offering, but lacking the arsenal depth or command to face a lineup multiple times as a starter. SIRPs carry the most leverage per inning of any pitcher role; the trade-off is they cover the fewest innings, so even an elite SIRP rarely projects above FV 50-55. Higher leverage than MIRP, fewer innings.

entries.definition: Multi-Inning Relief Pitcher - long relief, bulk follower, or swingman (~2+ innings per outing).
entries.methodology: Multi-Inning Relief Pitcher. FanGraphs designates a pitcher MIRP when their projected role is 2+ innings per outing - long-relief, bulk follower behind an opener, or true swingman. Typically prospects with starter-quality stuff but a command profile or arsenal depth issue that pushes them out of the rotation. MIRPs cover more innings than SIRPs but carry less leverage per inning; their FV ceiling sits between a true SP (deeper arsenal) and a SIRP (more leverage). The 'opener' phenomenon expanded the MIRP role's prominence over the last decade.

entries.definition: Future Value, the 20-80 scouting grade for a prospect's projected MLB ceiling.
entries.methodology: Every tracked source (FanGraphs, MLB Pipeline, ESPN, Just Baseball, TJStats, Baseball America, The Athletic) publishes a 20-80 grade per prospect. The site combines them into an accuracy-weighted consensus FV - per-source vote weights from each source's measured track record, shrunk hard toward equal so today only MLB Pipeline (1.06) and FanGraphs (0.94) differ from one vote - with Bayesian shrinkage applied to single-instance grades. FV 50 is a projected MLB regular, FV 60 is a first-division regular or future star, FV 70+ is perennial all-star ceiling.
entries.formula: consensus_fv = accuracy_weighted_mean(published_fvs) + shrinkage_pull · (FV_35 − mean) when only 1 instance exists
entries.example: Jackson Holliday's FV 65 means scouts collectively see him as a future star, one tier above an everyday regular but below a perennial all-star.

entries.definition: The standard scouting ladder. 20 = far below MLB, 50 = MLB average, 80 = elite.
entries.methodology: Scouting grades have been built on this scale since the 1950s. 50 is an MLB-average bench or role player, 60 is a first-division regular or All-Star, 70 is a perennial All-Star, 80 is a Hall-of-Fame ceiling. Used for individual tools (Hit, Power, Speed, Field, Throw, Fastball) and for overall Future Value.
entries.example: A 70-grade fastball means top ~5% of MLB starters. A 70-grade hit tool means batting-title contender.

entries.definition: 20-80 grade for bat-to-ball ability and projected batting average.
entries.methodology: Contact rate, plate coverage, pitch recognition, and projected batting average against MLB pitching. 50 ≈ .260 BA, 60 ≈ .290, 70 ≈ .320 ceiling.

entries.definition: 20-80 grade for in-game power output (HRs and extra-base hits).
entries.methodology: How much of a hitter's raw power actually plays in games, given swing path, pitch recognition, and approach. Almost always ≤ raw power for the same player.

entries.definition: 20-80 grade for BP / theoretical max power, regardless of in-game application.
entries.methodology: What a hitter can do at peak: exit velocity, BP home-run distance, peak EV. Different from game power, which folds in whether the swing actually unlocks the raw tool in competition.

entries.definition: 20-80 grade for foot speed. 60-yard dash, home-to-first time, baserunning instincts. Displayed as RUN across the site (the legacy abbreviation SPD also resolves).
entries.methodology: Plays on both sides of the ball: offense (baserunning, BABIP, extra bases) and defense (range, jumps, recovery). Run contributes to both the offensive (O-Tool, 4% weight) and defensive (D-Tool, 10% weight for non-catchers) composites for hitters.

entries.definition: 20-80 grade for defense; range, hands, instincts, throwing accuracy.
entries.methodology: Grades are position-relative. A 60 Field at SS isn't the same skill ceiling as a 60 Field at 1B. The 50 anchor is 'plays an average MLB-level version of the position.'

entries.definition: 20-80 grade for arm strength and accuracy.
entries.methodology: Critical for OF, SS, 3B, C; less weighted at 1B and 2B. 60+ is a legitimate plus arm, 70+ is elite (Andruw Jones, Yadier Molina caliber).

entries.definition: A prospect becomes 'Debuted' the moment MLB records their first MLB game.
entries.methodology: The MLB API's mlbDebutDate is the source of truth - when that field is set on a prospect's record, they move out of the active prospect pool and onto the Debuted tab. The site additionally promotes any prospect who has been outrighted (cleared waivers off the 40-man) since being on the 40-man already makes them a non-prospect. When neither signal is available, debut date falls back to the player's earliest MLB-season Opening Day from career stats. The rookie-eligibility thresholds (130 AB / 50 IP / 45 active-roster days) are NOT used - they produced unreliable dates whenever any upstream input was stale.
entries.formula: debuted iff mlbDebutDate is set OR an outright transaction is on file

entries.definition: League- and park-adjusted offensive value. 100 = MLB average.
entries.methodology: 100 is exactly league-average run creation. 120 is 20% above, 80 is 20% below. Park-adjusted and league-adjusted. MLB-only on this site; MiLB equivalents use the level-relative RPS+ proxy.

entries.definition: On-base Plus Slugging; OBP + SLG. The simplest catch-all hitter rate.
entries.methodology: .700 is below average, .800 is an above-average regular, .900+ is star-level. Doesn't park-adjust or league-adjust; use wRC+ for that.
entries.formula: OPS = OBP + SLG

entries.definition: Isolated Power, SLG minus AVG. Pure power rate.
entries.methodology: Strips singles out of slugging by subtracting batting average. .140 is average MLB power, .200 is above-average, .250+ is elite. Normalizes power across hitters with very different contact profiles.
entries.formula: ISO = SLG − AVG

entries.definition: Batting Average. Hits divided by at-bats.
entries.methodology: H / AB. Doesn't reward walks, doesn't distinguish singles from homers. Still useful as a contact-quality signal. .260 to .270 is MLB average, .300+ is above average.

entries.definition: On-base Percentage. Times reached base (H + BB + HBP) divided by plate appearances.
entries.methodology: Captures contact and discipline together. .330 is MLB average, .380+ is elite. Doesn't include reached-on-error.

entries.definition: Slugging Percentage. Total bases per at-bat; weights extra-base hits.
entries.methodology: (1B + 2·2B + 3·3B + 4·HR) / AB. .425 is MLB average, .500+ is above-average, .550+ is elite.

entries.definition: Walk rate. Walks divided by plate appearances.
entries.methodology: ~8% is MLB average, 12%+ is elite. Sticky across levels; a strong walk rate at A+ usually persists into AAA and MLB.
entries.formula: BB% = BB / PA

entries.definition: Strikeout rate. Strikeouts divided by plate appearances; lower is better for hitters.
entries.methodology: MLB average is ~22%. Sub-18% is above-average contact, 28%+ is a swing-and-miss concern. Mostly sticky across levels.
entries.formula: K% = K / PA

entries.definition: Earned Run Average. Earned runs allowed per 9 innings.
entries.methodology: Doesn't park-adjust or defense-adjust. 4.00 is MLB average, sub-3.50 is above-average, sub-3.00 is elite. Use FIP or xFIP for a defense-independent read.
entries.formula: ERA = ER · 9 / IP

entries.definition: Fielding-Independent Pitching. ERA-scaled, using only K, BB, HBP, HR.
entries.methodology: What a pitcher's ERA would be with league-average luck on balls in play. ~4.00 is MLB average. Use FIP- for the 100-anchored version.
entries.formula: FIP = ((13·HR) + 3·(BB+HBP) − 2·K) / IP + constant

entries.definition: Walks + Hits per Inning Pitched. Baserunner volume.
entries.methodology: (BB + H) / IP. 1.30 is MLB average, sub-1.20 is above average, sub-1.10 is elite. Combines walk rate and contact-quality allowed.
entries.formula: WHIP = (BB + H) / IP

entries.definition: Expected FIP. FIP using league-average HR/FB rate instead of actual HR allowed.
entries.methodology: Strips out HR luck. More predictive year-over-year than FIP. ~4.00 is MLB average, sub-3.50 is above-average.

entries.definition: Park- and league-adjusted FIP scaled to 100 = MLB average. Lower is better.
entries.methodology: 100 is league-average run prevention (defense-independent), 80 is 20% better (top-tier), 120 is 20% worse. Inverts the usual 'higher = better' convention because lower run prevention is better.

entries.definition: Strikeouts per 9 innings - legacy metric; this site now uses K% (per-batter) as the canonical strikeout rate.
entries.methodology: 9 K/9 is MLB average for a starter, 11+ is elite. K% (per-batter) is more workload-stable than K/9 (per-inning) since starter and reliever IP-per-appearance differ widely. As of v22 the site surfaces K% everywhere; K/9 is only used as a fallback when batters-faced isn't on file for an older MiLB row.
entries.formula: K/9 = K · 9 / IP

entries.definition: Walks per 9 innings - legacy metric; this site now uses BB% (per-batter) as the canonical walk rate.
entries.methodology: 3.0 BB/9 is MLB average, sub-2.5 is above average, sub-2.0 is elite command. BB% is preferred because it normalizes for IP-per-appearance differences (starters vs relievers). As of v22 the site surfaces BB% everywhere; BB/9 is only a fallback when batters-faced is missing from a career row.
entries.formula: BB/9 = BB · 9 / IP

entries.definition: Home runs allowed per 9 innings.
entries.methodology: ~1.3 HR/9 is MLB average, sub-1.0 is above average. Heavily park- and league-dependent.
entries.formula: HR/9 = HR · 9 / IP

entries.definition: Pitcher strikeout rate. Strikeouts as % of batters faced. Canonical strikeout metric site-wide (replaced K/9 in v22).
entries.methodology: Preferred over K/9 because per-batter rate doesn't depend on starter vs reliever IP-per-appearance. ~22% is MLB average, 28%+ is elite. When batters-faced isn't on file for a career row, the value is approximated from K/9 via the league-average ~4.3 batters/inning conversion.
entries.formula: K% = K / TBF (fallback: K/9 ÷ 0.387 when TBF missing)

entries.definition: Pitcher walk rate. Walks as % of batters faced. Canonical walk metric site-wide (replaced BB/9 in v22).
entries.methodology: Preferred over BB/9 - same reasoning as K%. ~8% is MLB average, sub-7% above average, sub-6% elite command. Approximated from BB/9 ÷ 0.387 when batters-faced isn't on file.
entries.formula: BB% = BB / TBF (fallback: BB/9 ÷ 0.387 when TBF missing)

entries.definition: Wins Above Replacement - Baseball-Reference's implementation (bWAR) is the one WAR source used site-wide. Single-number value estimate covering offense, defense, baserunning, and position.
entries.methodology: Baseball-Reference's implementation (bWAR) is the one WAR source used site-wide - career totals, per-season columns, and current-season pills all read the same per-season series. 2 WAR/yr is an MLB regular, 4 is an above-average regular, 6+ is All-Star, 8+ is MVP candidate. Used as the realized output baseline for WAG.

entries.definition: The site-computed FV; an accuracy-weighted mean of all source publications with single-instance shrinkage.
entries.methodology: For every snapshot, the consensus FV is an accuracy-weighted mean of explicit FVs published by any tracked source. When only one source has ever published the player (across their entire history, not just the latest snapshot), the consensus is Bayesian-pulled 1/3 toward FV 35 to reflect single-observation uncertainty. The pull lifts as soon as a second grade lands, even from the same source. Phase 4 (2026-06): the blend is ACCURACY-WEIGHTED - relative vote weights from each source's measured track record on resolved common-set cohorts (vintage-disciplined: a board year only uses track records resolvable before it), shrunk hard toward equal (k=150) and clamped [0.6, 1.5]. Current weights: MLB Pipeline 1.06, FanGraphs 0.94 - the resolved cohorts measured Pipeline slightly ahead, the opposite of the popular prior; sources without resolved history vote at 1.0. Shipped only after the weighted blend beat equal-weight on both pooled Spearman and AUC in the A/B (data/consensus_weight_eval.json); disagreement metrics stay unweighted.
entries.formula:
consensus FV = accuracy-weighted mean(latest explicit FV from each tracked source)
single-source case: shrunk = (n_obs · src_FV + k · prior_FV) / (n_obs + k)
entries.example: A prospect carrying 60/62/65 grades across five sources lands at an accuracy-weighted consensus of about 62, with the 60-65 spread (stddev 2.4) shown as the Wide Spread marker when it stretches. A rank-implied FV that reads higher than the published grades is a gap the Source Comparison tab surfaces.

entries.definition: Trailing-window FV trajectory; direction and delta since the player's prior snapshot.
entries.methodology: Compares latest consensus_fv_raw against the prior point in the player's history. ▲ is up by ≥1.5 FV, ▼ is down, - is flat. Shows up on list rows and as a stock chip in the detail-page header.
entries.formula:
stock = consensus_fv_raw(latest) − consensus_fv_raw(prior snapshot)
▲ if ≥ +1.5 · ▼ if ≤ −1.5 · "-" otherwise
entries.example: A prospect whose consensus moves 48 to 50 between snapshots shows ▲ +2 on his row; a 48 to 47.5 move stays flat ("-") (under the 1.5-point gate, so source noise does not read as news).

entries.definition: Composite rank of all 30 MLB farm systems. 45% top-end + 25% depth + 15% trajectory + 15% grad pipeline.
entries.methodology: Each component scored 0-100 across the 30 orgs, then blended. Top-end is a tiered FV-points sum of the top 5 prospects (an FV 80 worth ~100× an FV 40). Depth is the same sum for prospects 6 through 25. Trajectory is 1y DvM+. Grad pipeline is FV-weighted debuts in the trailing 12 months.
entries.formula: farm_score = 0.45·top_end + 0.25·depth + 0.15·trajectory + 0.15·grad_pipeline
entries.example: The 2026-06 board has the Dodgers at #1 with a farm score of 117: an elite top five (Josue De Paula FV 57 leads), top-25 depth, positive 1y DvM+ trajectory, and a productive graduate pipeline. Farm scores read like wRC+: 100 is the league-mean system, 117 is about 1.7 standard deviations above it.

entries.definition: Estimated MLB arrival year. Derived from level, age vs level mean, and FV grade adjustments.
entries.methodology: Starts from the current-level baseline (AAA ≈ 0.8 yr to MLB, AA ≈ 1.5 yr, A+ ≈ 2.5 yr) and applies adjustments for performance (RPS+ vs level), age vs level mean, FV grade, and IL/health flags. Confidence label (high / mid / low) reflects the spread between the components.
entries.formula:
years_to_MLB = level_base + perf_adj + age_adj + fv_adj + health_adj
ETA year = current season + ceil(years_to_MLB, by season phase)
entries.example: Ryan Sloan (SEA, AA): base 1.35y for AA, +0.5 performance, −1.15 age-vs-level (young for AA), −0.25 FV-grade leaves about 0.45y, so the board shows ETA 2027 at high confidence. Every term is visible in the ETA tooltip on his card.

entries.definition: FV-toward-35 pull applied when a prospect has only one published grade in their entire history.
entries.methodology: k=0.5 Bayesian shrinkage: consensus = (2/3 · raw_FV) + (1/3 · 35). The FV badge for single-instance prospects carries a dashed amber outline plus a small '1' mark. A FanGraphs-only prospect graded multiple times across snapshots is well-observed and is NOT shrunken; only true single-observations get the pull.
entries.formula: if total_fv_instances ≤ 1: pulled_fv = (2/3) · raw_fv + (1/3) · 35

entries.definition: Purple 'W' mark on the FV badge; sources disagree by ≥10 grade points (a two-tier gap).
entries.methodology: When 2+ sources have published the player and their max-min spread is ≥10 grade points (e.g., FG 45 vs Pipeline 55), the FV badge carries a violet 'W' corner mark. Hover for the spread and source count. Means the consensus averages meaningfully disagreeing views, a 'wide read' rather than tight consensus.

entries.definition: Total $M of MLB value above cost-controlled salary. Two distinct flavors: PROJECTED (prospects, FV-derived) and REALIZED (debutants/MLB, actual career WAR-derived).
entries.methodology:
v32.1 - Two distinct measurements depending on which side of debut a player is on, kept strictly separate:
• **Projected** (prospects, pre-debut): FV → projected WAR → projected $ via the value_framework formula (Sur+). Granular at any FV (47, 52.3, etc).
• **Realized** (debutants / MLB players): actual career WAR × $/WAR_overall ($11.74M rolling 3yr 2024-2026 avg) minus actual or estimated salaries paid. Positive means the team beat the bet implied by the player's grade; negative means they paid more than the realized value.
These are NEVER mixed in a single $/FV ratio (vets don't have a meaningful FV anchor). Trade audits surface them side-by-side: 'Org A received 15 FV-pts projected at $1.7M/FV-pt + $48M realized vet value'.

v3 - the $/WAR LEVEL re-anchors at load to the FA module's signings-implied series (data/fa_dpw_series.json: what clubs actually paid per discounted projected win on the open market, the Gate-2-validated estimator), trailing-3-winter mean, tier shape preserved. Open-market $/WAR is the basis for surplus: it prices what the wins would otherwise cost to buy. Each control season still escalates with $/WAR inflation and discounts at 9%. Phase 4 (2026-06): a REAL-data calibration layer now corrects the raw mixture model's measured margin overshoot (first real backtest: 2,958 prospects from 2017-19 listings; raw calibration slope 0.64, i.e. ~$1.6 predicted per $1 realized at the margin). The isotonic correction was validated leave-one-year-out (held-out slope 0.96, bias -0.1M, P10-P90 coverage 0.86) and is applied to every published surplus number; backtests always re-fit against the raw layer. Headline effect: an FV-55 hitter's expected surplus moved from ~$41M to ~$22M, matching what a 55 has historically returned.

Calibration (v3, 2026-06-12): the career-path mixture's raw expectation is corrected by a monotone map fit on what 2017-19 listed prospects ACTUALLY returned over their control years, with realized WAR valued at the standing $/WAR rate (not the cheaper rates of those seasons). The number reads as expected realized value at current replacement cost, in the same units as veteran surplus - a 50 FV hitter calibrates to roughly $18M, a 60 FV to the mid-$60M range.

entries.definition: Average Annual Value. Total contract value divided by years.
entries.methodology: For deferral-heavy deals (e.g., Ohtani's $700M / 10yr but only ~$46M present-value AAV) the displayed AAV is the present-value-adjusted figure, not raw money divided by years.

entries.definition: Per-team amateur signing budget. Separate IFA pool and draft pool ceilings per year.
entries.methodology: Draft pool is the sum of the team's first-10-rounds slot values. IFA pool is the MLB-assigned international signing budget (base ~$5.95M plus competitive-balance bonuses). Teams can exceed by up to ~5% before luxury-tax penalties kick in.

entries.definition: MLB-assigned bonus value for an individual draft pick. Sums into the team's draft pool ceiling.
entries.methodology: Every pick in the first 10 rounds has a published slot value. Teams can sign over slot for top picks if they sign under for later picks (rebalancing within the pool). Going over the pool total triggers a tax plus potential future-pick penalty.

entries.definition: Major League Baseball. The top tier; the destination for every prospect's projection.
Triple-A. The last level before MLB; many AAA prospects are MLB call-up candidates.
entries.methodology: International League (Eastern AAA) and Pacific Coast League (Western AAA). Avg age ~26. Most AAA players are 4A vets, but young AAA performers (≤24) are typically near-term MLB candidates.

entries.definition: Double-A. The level where prospect projections become real; the hardest development jump.
entries.methodology: Texas, Eastern, and Southern Leagues. Avg age ~23. AA is the level where pitching quality and breaking-ball usage start to approximate MLB conditions. Prospects who succeed at AA usually carry their performance forward.

entries.definition: High-A. The second full-season level above Single-A.
entries.methodology: Avg age ~22. Most college draftees start here; HS draftees usually arrive after a year of A-ball.

entries.definition: Low-A / Single-A. The first full-season level.
entries.methodology: Avg age ~21. The first level of structured 130+ game seasons after the complex or DSL.

entries.definition: Complex League. Short-season rookie ball at the team's spring-training complex.
entries.methodology: Avg age ~19. Most HS draftees and recent IFAs get their first stateside reps in the CPX.

entries.definition: Dominican Summer League - the entry point for most international amateur signings. Players are 16-19, mostly IFAs.
entries.methodology: Affiliated rookie ball played in the Dominican Republic; avg age ~18, heavily Latin American (Dominican, Venezuelan, Colombian signees). Each MLB org runs at least one DSL team and many run two. DSL → complex league (CPX) → A-ball is the typical international development ladder.

entries.definition: International Free Agent. Amateur players signed from outside the U.S., Canada, and Puerto Rico.
entries.methodology: Each org has a fixed annual IFA bonus pool. Players sign at 16 from Latin America (heavy DR and VZ representation), Asia (KBO and NPB posting after age 25), Cuba, and elsewhere. Top IFAs get bonuses in the $3-5M range.

entries.definition: Player is recovering from Tommy John (UCL replacement) elbow surgery. ~14-18 month recovery typical.
entries.methodology: Tommy John (ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction) is the most common pitching surgery. Recovery curve: 0-6mo throwing, 6-12mo mound work, 12-14mo rehab assignments, 14-18mo MLB return. Roughly 80% of TJ recipients return to prior form within 2 years; ~10% never pitch at the same level again.

entries.definition: Player is currently on the active Injured List. Multiple IL types: 7-day, 10-day, 15-day, 60-day.
entries.methodology: 60-day IL freezes a player's 40-man roster slot. 15-day IL is the standard major-injury duration. The site surfaces every IL stint over the trailing 12 months; the Health profile aggregates the count and total IL days.

entries.definition: 20-80 scouting grade for a pitcher's fastball - velocity, movement, shape, and command of the pitch.
entries.methodology: Most pitchers' headline tool. 60+ is plus (mid-90s + ride or sink); 70+ is plus-plus (upper-90s + carry). The grade folds together velo, vertical/horizontal break, and command of the pitch; pure velo without shape rarely earns above 55.

entries.definition: 20-80 grade for the pitcher's slider (or sweeper variant) - sharpness, depth, tunneling with the fastball.
entries.methodology: Sliders sit ~5-10 mph below the FB; sweepers add ~15-18 inches of horizontal break. Both ride the 'sl' slot in our data because their roles overlap. 60+ is a true out-pitch slider; 50 is average MLB shape.

entries.definition: 20-80 grade for the curveball - depth, shape, and command of the slowest breaking pitch.
entries.methodology: Distinct from a slider by velocity (8-12 mph slower than the FB vs. 5-10) and by primarily vertical break. Spike/knuckle/standard grips all map to 'cb' in our data. 60+ curveballs typically pair with a deep FB slot (over-the-top arm action).

entries.definition: 20-80 grade for the changeup (or splitter) - velo separation, arm-action deception, and command.
entries.methodology: Changeups sit 8-12 mph below the FB with sink/fade. Splitters sit 8-12 mph below with hard tumble - different grip, same role in the arsenal. Both ride the 'ch' slot. 60+ changeups define a starter's profile vs. lefties.

entries.definition: 20-80 grade for the ability to locate pitches WITHIN the strike zone (not just throw strikes).
entries.methodology: Control = ability to throw strikes; Command = ability to throw the right strike. Plus command (60+) means consistently spotting the FB on the corner, burying the breaker below the zone, etc. Most prospects sit 45-50; a 60 command grade dramatically lifts the ceiling.

entries.definition: 20-80 grade for the cutter - a hybrid between FB and slider with late horizontal break, ~3-5 mph below the FB.
entries.methodology: FG and Pipeline don't always grade the cutter as a distinct slot; Just Baseball does. We carry 'ct' as a canonical key so JB-graded cutters flow into consensus when published. The pitch's role is FB-like (in-zone, two-strike strike-out option) but with arm-side cut.

entries.definition: 20-80 grade for a hitter's swing decisions and pitch recognition - chase / contact rate / zone awareness.
entries.methodology: A separate skill from the hit tool (bat-to-ball). 60+ pitch selection means low chase, high z-contact, willingness to take walks. FG publishes this as a standalone grade; Just Baseball calls it 'Plate Disc.'. Feeds the offensive composite alongside Hit / Game Power.

entries.definition: 20-80 grade for barrel control - the ability to manipulate the bat in-zone, foul off tough pitches, square balls up.
entries.methodology: Distinct from the broader hit tool. Bat control speaks to swing path quality, bat-head awareness, and 2-strike adjustability - the difference between a plus hitter who barrels everything (60+) and one who hits .280 but chases the barrel (50).

entries.definition: MLB's December draft of minor leaguers left unprotected by their org. Selecting team must keep the player on its MLB 26-man all season or offer them back.
entries.methodology: Held during the Winter Meetings (early December). Any player signed at 18+ with 4 years of pro service, or at 19+ with 5 years, must be added to the 40-man roster by the Nov 20 protection deadline or risk Rule 5 selection. Picks cost $100K. Returning a Rule 5 pick costs the selecting team $50K.

entries.definition: The annual July amateur player draft - 20 rounds, picks from US/Canada/Puerto Rico HS and college. Distinct from the Rule 5 (Dec) draft.
entries.methodology: Each team has a bonus pool sized to their pick slot values; spending under pool saves nothing, spending over by >5% triggers picks-forfeiture penalties. International players (DSL/Latin America) don't go through Rule 4 - they sign as IFAs.

entries.definition: The 40 players a team can call up to MLB without exposing to other clubs. Drives Rule 5 protection deadlines.
entries.methodology: Includes the active 26-man + players on the 10/15-day IL + minor leaguers added to protect from Rule 5. The 60-day IL adds an EXTRA slot temporarily. Teams crunch to fit 40 every November; DFAs and trades shake players loose.

entries.definition: Each 40-man player has 3 (sometimes 4) option years allowing free MLB↔AAA shuttle. After they're used, the player must clear waivers to be sent down.
entries.methodology: An 'option' is burned the first time a player is sent to the minors in a season AND spends 20+ days there. Burning an option each of three seasons exhausts them. Out-of-options players are higher-stakes 40-man slots - they can't be sent down freely.

entries.definition: MLB days accrued on the active roster or IL. 172 days = 1 'year' of service. 3 yrs → arbitration; 6 yrs → free agency.
entries.methodology: The single biggest factor in a player's career economics. Teams routinely 'manipulate' service time by holding rookies in AAA for 2-3 weeks to preserve a year of team control. 'Super Two' is the additional ~22% of 2-yr players who reach arbitration a year early.

entries.definition: Salary process for players with 3-6 yrs of MLB service. Player + team file binding numbers; an arbitrator picks one if they don't settle.
entries.methodology: Arbitration cases are heard in February. The arbitrator picks ONE side's number - no splitting. Most cases settle before the hearing. Arb-year salaries scale up year over year (Yr1 ~$1M, Yr3 ~$8M for stars). Super Twos get a 4th arb year.

entries.definition: Service-time window from 0 to ~3 yrs MLB time. Player is paid at or near the league minimum with no salary leverage.
entries.methodology: Pre-arb is the most team-friendly part of a player's career - most graduates spend their first 2-3 MLB years here. Salaries are unilaterally set by the club (subject to league minimum, ~$760k in 2024). The new CBA introduced a Pre-Arb Bonus Pool that retroactively rewards top performers but doesn't change the unilateral-pay structure. Once the player crosses 3.000 of MLB service (or qualifies as Super Two), they enter arbitration.

entries.definition: Players in the top 22% of 2-3 service-year players get a 4th arbitration year. Costs the team an extra arb cycle.
entries.methodology: After each season, MLB identifies players with between 2.000 and 3.000 of service time. The top 22% by service days qualify as Super Two and become arb-eligible a year early. Teams aggressively manage call-ups to keep top prospects below the Super Two cutoff - usually requires keeping the player on the active roster for fewer than ~125 days in his first MLB season.

entries.definition: Strategic delay of a top prospect's MLB debut to gain an extra year of team control. Less common post-2022 CBA but not eliminated.
entries.methodology: If a club holds a prospect in AAA for the first ~3 weeks of the regular season, the player won't accumulate 172 days of MLB service that year - pushing free agency back by a year. The 2022 CBA introduced PPI (Prospect Promotion Incentive) draft picks for clubs that promote top prospects on Opening Day AND those players finish top-2 in ROY voting or top-5 in MVP/Cy Young - partially aligning incentives. Famous examples: Kris Bryant (2015 grievance lost), Vladimir Guerrero Jr. (2019 demotion).

entries.definition: Players with 6+ years of MLB service may sign with any club once the World Series ends; the first five days are an exclusive-negotiation window with the incumbent club and the qualifying-offer period.
entries.methodology: Major-league free agency requires 6.000 of service time. The 5-day window after the World Series is exclusive negotiating period with the prior team; after that, the player is open to all 30 clubs. Minor-league free agency is separate - minor-leaguers become 6-year MiLB FAs after their 6th professional season unless on a 40-man roster. Spotrac, MLB Trade Rumors, and Baseball-Reference all track FA classes by year.

entries.definition: One-year contract a club may offer its departing free agent at the mean of MLB's top-125 salaries (~$21M in 2024). If the player declines and signs elsewhere, the SIGNING club forfeits draft-pick compensation and the former club gains a comp pick - the offer itself costs the old club nothing beyond the one-year salary risk.
entries.methodology: Teams can extend a QO to free agents who spent the entire prior season with the team and haven't received one before. If the player declines (almost always) and signs elsewhere, the signing team forfeits draft picks; the losing team gets a compensation pick. The QO value is calculated annually as the simple average of the top 125 player salaries. Mid-season trade acquisitions are NOT QO-eligible (a key trade-deadline tax).

entries.definition: Extra draft picks awarded for QO-declined free agents, Prospect Promotion Incentive (PPI), and revenue-sharing balance.
entries.methodology: Two main sources: (1) QO comp - teams losing a QO'd FA get a pick after either round 1 (small-market teams) or after round 4 (mid/large markets, depending on luxury-tax status). The signing team forfeits a pick to balance. (2) PPI - clubs that promote a top prospect on Opening Day and the player wins ROY (or top-2) earn a pick after round 1. The Competitive Balance Lottery also awards 10-12 picks (Round A + Round B) to lower-revenue clubs.

entries.definition: Post-DFA path - player clears waivers and is sent off the 40-man roster down to AAA. Player can refuse if they have 3+ MLB service yrs.
entries.methodology: After a DFA, the team has 7 days. If the player clears waivers (no other club claims them), they can be outrighted to AAA. The player loses 40-man protection but keeps minor-league assignment rights. Players with 3+ MLB service years OR a prior outright in their career can REFUSE the outright and elect free agency. Each outright stays on the player's record permanently.

entries.definition: Removal from the 40-man roster. Team has 7 days to trade, waive, or release the player. A common 40-man crunch mechanism.
entries.methodology: A DFA freezes the player off the active roster and starts the 7-day clock. Outcomes: outright to AAA (player can refuse if they have 3+ MLB service yrs), waiver claim (any other team grabs them), trade, or release. Most DFA'd players clear waivers and accept the outright.

entries.definition: First MLB appearance. Per the v21 debut rule, mlbDebutDate being set moves a prospect to the Debuted tab.
entries.methodology: We mark MLB debuts with a ★ chip on the transaction-history table. Pre-debut, a prospect's value is theoretical; post-debut, the FV starts converting to (or away from) real MLB performance. Debut removes a player from the active prospect lists and surfaces them on the Debuted tab.

entries.definition: Lump-sum payment at signing for amateur players. Draftees pull from the team's draft pool; IFAs from the IFA pool.
entries.methodology: Draft slot values are published each year by MLB. Teams can spend up to 5% over pool with progressive tax penalties; >5% costs future first-round picks. IFA bonuses are capped at the assigned pool size (~$5.95M base + competitive-balance bonuses) - no overage allowed since 2017.

entries.definition: Three IL durations: 10-day (position players), 15-day (the minimum for pitchers and two-way players, post-2022), and 60-day, which also frees the player's 40-man roster spot.
entries.methodology: A team can transfer between IL types - a 15-day IL stint can convert to 60-day when the player misses more time. The 60-day IL removes the player from the 40-man count (extra roster flexibility). Concussion IL is a separate 7-day version.

entries.definition: Official MLB designation: 20+ MLB innings pitched AND 20+ MLB games started as a position player or DH with at least 3 plate appearances in each. Qualifying exempts the player from the pitcher-usage rules that bar position players from pitching in competitive games.
entries.methodology: Ohtani is the canonical example. The site detects two-way profiles when a prospect has both hitter (hit/game_pwr/...) AND pitcher (fb/sl/...) canonical tool grades - both Tools cards then render. Reggie Crawford and a handful of recent draftees fit the pattern.

entries.definition: Scouting grades come in pairs: present grade (what they show today) and future grade (projected peak). FG ships them as 'Hit 30/55' = present 30, future 55.
entries.methodology: We always store the FUTURE grade as the canonical tool number (the projection is the actionable signal). Present grades ride alongside in _extras['present'] for sources that publish both. The gap between present and future encodes risk / development runway.

entries.definition: Rookie-level stateside ball played at team training complexes (Arizona or Florida). Mostly recent draftees + DSL graduates.
entries.methodology: Two leagues: ACL (Arizona Complex League, ex-AZL) and FCL (Florida Complex League, ex-GCL). Games at team backfields, no fans. Players are 17-20. The 2021 MiLB reorg consolidated the older rookie-level leagues into these two.

entries.definition: Green ▲ = consensus FV rose since the last update; red ▼ = fell. Magnitude is the FV-delta.
entries.methodology: Drives the 'Up' / 'Down' filter on the Active list. Stock reads as 'delta since the most recent prior update' - a player with only one update reads as 'flat'. Movements ≥ 1.5 grade-points show in the row's meta line.

entries.definition: Color-coded chip showing the player's consensus Future Value. Red = elite (70+), orange = high (60-65), yellow = mid (50-55), grey = lower (40-45).
entries.visual: 70605045

entries.definition: Animated border treatment around player headshots / cards. Anchored at FV 40 (average prospect - no treatment); every tier above 40 picks up a richer foil/chrome/holo shimmer.
entries.methodology:
Rarity ramp anchored at FV 40 (baseline) with HOLO above CHROME (chrome is static silver; holo carries the rainbow shift, so the rainbow tier reads as rarer). Five rarity bands above the baseline, mirroring the Topps Chrome / refractor aesthetic:\
 • FV 70+ → LEGENDARY · animated rainbow with pulsing outline glow (top ~1%)\
 • FV 61-69 → HOLO · full rainbow shift (plus prospect, above first-division floor)\
 • FV 55-60 → CHROME · silver shimmer (FV 60 first-division floor lives here)\
 • FV 50-54 → FOIL · faint silver foil (MLB-regular projection)\
 • FV 45-49 → SHINE · static gold ring (above-average org piece)\
 • FV 40 → baseline, no treatment (average prospect)\
 • FV < 40 → no treatment\
Applied everywhere a player headshot or card renders - list rows, spotlight cards, the prospect detail page header, compare view.

entries.definition: Pill on the row showing Tool composite. Green ≥60 (Plus), neutral ≥50 (avg), amber ≥40 (below avg), red <40. 20-80 scouting scale.
entries.visual: Tool 65Tool 52Tool 45Tool 38
